extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and readers of classical mechanics (Newton's Principia)
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of foundational propositions and mathematical lemmas from Newton's Principia (De Motu Corporum, Liber I): geometric-method statements and physical laws about motion, collisions, center of gravity, and areas swept by radii.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitas motus non mutatur ab actione corporum inter se (Conservation of motion / momentum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitas motus quæ colligitur capiendo summam motuum factorum ad eandem partem, & differentiam factorum ad contrarias, non mutatur ab actione corporum inter se.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement and proof that in collisions the algebraic sum (sum of motions in one direction and difference for opposite directions) remains unchanged by mutual actions. Includes detailed numerical-style examples (spherical bodies A and B with parts of motion) showing how post-collision motion parts redistribute while the total (sum/difference combination) remains the same. Also addresses oblique collisions by resolving motions into components perpendicular and parallel to the tangent plane and shows conservation applies componentwise. Guidance includes method for computing post-collision velocities by comparing pre/post 'motus parts' ratios and using component decomposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commune gravitatis centrum ab actionibus internis non mutatur (Center of gravity motion invariant under internal actions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commune gravitatis centrum ab actionibus corporum inter se non mutat statum suum vel motus vel quietis, & propterea corporum omnium in se mutuo agentium (exclusis actionibus & impedimentis externis) commune centrum gravitatis vel quiescit vel movetur uniformiter in directum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstration that internal forces cannot change the motion (state of rest or uniform motion) of the system's center of gravity. Argument proceeds by induction on numbers of bodies: for two bodies it uses reciprocal proportionality of distances to the center and equality of relative motions; extends to many-body systems by composition. Practical implication: motion of a system can be characterized by motion of its center of mass; internal interactions do not alter that motion unless external forces act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relativity of uniform translation (Galilean relativity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporum dato spatio inclusorum ijdem sunt motus inter se, sive spatium illud quiescat, sive moveatur idem uniformiter in directum absq; motu circulari.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a set of bodies occupies a given space, their mutual motions are the same whether the containing space is at rest or is moving uniformly in a straight line. The text notes the equality of relative effects (collisions, impulses) and gives the ship experiment example: motions behave the same on a ship whether it is at rest or moving uniformly. Useful as a criterion for invariance of mechanical experiments under uniform translation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal parallel accelerative forces do not change relative motions
rubrics_metrics.description: Si corpora moveantur quomodocunq; inter se & a viribus acceleratricibus æqualibus secundum lineas parallelas urgeantur; pergent omnia eodem modo moveri inter se ac si viribus illis non essent incitata.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If all bodies are subject to equal accelerative forces in parallel directions (proportional to masses so that accelerations are equal), their mutual motions remain as if those forces were absent. The corollary formalizes that equal parallel accelerations cancel out for relative motion, preserving relative positions and velocities between bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lex tertia motus: actioni contrariae reactio aequales (Third law / action equals reaction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Actio eiq; contraria reactio æquales sunt per Legem 3, adeoq; per legem 2, æquales in motibus efficiunt mutationes versus contrarias partes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholium and discussion: statement of third law with experimental corroboration (pendulum experiments) and consequences for collisions and machines. Includes guidance about perfect vs imperfect elasticity: in perfectly elastic collisions relative rebound velocity equals approach velocity; in imperfect elasticity rebound velocity is reduced in proportion to the elastic force. Examples: pendulum and ball collision experiments measuring ratios (e.g., wool balls ratio ~5:9, steel ~similar, glass ~15:16). Also uses magnet/iron experiment to illustrate mutual attraction equality. Discusses implications for machines: forces transmitted through instruments produce equal and opposite reactions; determination of effectiveness of machines rests on reciprocal relation of forces and velocities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of prime and ultimate ratios (foundational limit method)
rubrics_metrics.description: De Methodo Rationum primarum & ultimarum, cujus ope sequentia demonstrantur. Lemma I: Quantitates, ut & quantitatum rationes, quæ ad æqualitatem dato tempore constanter tendunt & eo pacto propius ad invicem accedere possunt quam pro data quavis differentia; fiunt ultimo æquales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma I states the basic principle of limits: if two quantities (or ratios) approach equality so that for any given difference they can be made closer, then their ultimate ratio is equality. This is Newton's justification for using limits (method of prime and ultimate ratios) instead of indivisibles. Guidance explains interpreting 'ultimate' ratio at the instant quantities vanish or are born, and defends geometric limiting processes to avoid indivisible hypothesis. Use-case: justifies later limit-based geometric demonstrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inscribed and circumscribed parallelogram approximations converge (Lemma II and III)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lemma II & III: If in a figure parallelograms are inscribed and circumscribed under equal bases and widths diminished to zero with number increased to infinity, the ultimate ratios of the inscribed, circumscribed and the curvilinear figure are ratios of equality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows that sums of inscribed and circumscribed rectangles (parallelograms) converge to the same area as widths shrink and their number increases. Corollaries: sums of vanishing parallelograms coincide with the curved figure; straight-line polygons formed by chords or tangents converge to the curve's limit. This is the geometric underpinning of area/arc limit arguments used later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit-preservation of ratios between two figures using parallelogram series (Lemma IV)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two figures have corresponding series of parallelograms with the same number and whose widths diminish to zero, and the ultimate ratios of corresponding parallelograms are the same, then the figures are in that same ultimate ratio to one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma IV demonstrates that if corresponding infinitesimal parts of two figures are ultimately proportional, then the whole figures are ultimately proportional. Application: comparing areas, perimeters, or other aggregated measures by comparing small corresponding elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity and area proportionality for similar figures (Lemma V)
rubrics_metrics.description: Similium figurarum latera omnia, quæ sibi mutuo respondent, sunt proportionalia, tam curvilinea quam rectilinea, & areæ sunt in duplicata ratione laterum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States that corresponding sides of similar figures (including curvilinear ones) are proportional and their areas are in the duplicate (square) ratio of corresponding sides. Used to relate areas to linear measures in limit arguments and geometric similarity reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chord–tangent angle vanishes as points coalesce (Lemma VI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Si arcus quilibet positione datus AB subtendatur chorda AB, & in puncto aliquo A, in medio curvaturæ continuæ, tangatur a recta utrinq; producta AD; ... dico quod angulus BAD sub chorda & tangente contentus minuetur in infinitum & ultimo evanescet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows that the angle between the chord and the tangent tends to zero as chord endpoints approach the tangency point. Used to justify replacing small arcs by their chords or tangents in limiting geometric constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ultimate ratios of arc, chord, and tangent are equal (Lemma VII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Iisdem positis, dico quod ultima ratio arcus, chordæ & tangentis ad invicem est ratio æqualitatis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishes that in the limit of vanishing arcs, the lengths of the arc, its chord, and the tangent segment are ultimately equal in ratio. Corollaries show ultimate equality of various abscissae and that these lines can be used interchangeably in limit proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vanishing infinitesimal triangles become similar (Lemma VIII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Si rectæ datæ AR, BR cum arcu AB, chorda AB & tangente AD, triangula tria ARB, ARB, ARD constituunt, dein puncta A, B accedunt ad invicem: dico quod ultima forma triangulorum evanescentium est similitudinis, & ultima ratio æqualitatis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When points coalesce, the small triangles formed by lines and tangents/chords become similar in the ultimate form; thus small triangle arguments preserve similarity in the limit. Application: replacing infinitesimal curved segments by linear approximations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Areas of small triangles approach duplicate ratio of corresponding sides (Lemma IX)
rubrics_metrics.description: Si recta AE & Curva AC positione datæ se mutuo secent in angulo dato A, & ad rectam illam in alio dato angulo ordinatim applicentur BD, EC, curvæ occurrentes in B, C; dein puncta B, C accedant ad punctum A: dico quod areæ triangulorum ADB, AEC erunt ultimo ad invicem in duplicata ratione laterum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As two points on a curve approach the base point, the areas of associated triangles are in the duplicate ratio of the sides (i.e., proportional to square of corresponding linear measure). Used to relate areas under velocity ordinates to time-squared in kinematic derivations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformly accelerated motion: spaces ∝ times^2 (Lemma X)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spatia, quæ corpus urgente quacunq; vi regulari describit, sunt ipso motus initio in duplicata ratione temporum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States that for motion generated by a regular (i.e., uniformly accelerating) force, the distances described from the start are in the duplicate (square) ratio of the times; i.e., s ∝ t^2. Proof uses areas under velocity ordinates and Lemma IX. Corollary: errors produced by similar forces applied to similar bodies scale as forces × time^2 (useful for dimensional reasoning in kinematics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between vanishing subtended contact and arc (Lemma XI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subtensa evanescens anguli contactus est ultimo in ratione duplicata subtensæ arcus contermini.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives a limit relation: as the angle of contact (angle between tangent and a chord) vanishes, its subtending length is ultimately in the duplicate ratio of the adjacent arc. Corollaries connect tangent/chord/sine squared relations and triangle area ratios, used in careful limiting geometry for curvature-related arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Areas swept by radius are proportional to times (Proposition I, Theorem I)
rubrics_metrics.description: Areas quas corpora in gyros acta radiis ad immobile centrum virium ductis describunt, & in planis immobilibus consistere, & esse temporibus proportionales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrates that the area swept by the radius vector to a fixed center is proportional to the time: equal times correspond to equal areas. Proof by discretizing time into equal parts and using equal triangular areas, then passing to the limit. Corollaries: in non-resisting media, if areas are not proportional to times then forces do not point to the same center; if areas accelerate, forces diverge from a common center. Practical usage: foundation of planetary area law (Kepler's second law) and relation between centripetal forces and area rates.
